title: Chapter 67 — Cutting In
paragraphs: It was a Saturday night, and such a Sabbath as followed! By their very profession, all whalemen are breakers of the Sabbath. The ivory Pequod was turned into what seemed a slaughterhouse. Every sailor was a butcher. You would have thought we were sacrificing ten thousand red oxen to the sea gods.

In the first place, the enormous cutting tackles were hoisted up to the main-top. Among other ponderous things, they include a cluster of blocks generally painted green, which no single man can possibly lift; and this vast bunch of grapes was firmly lashed to the lower masthead, the strongest point anywhere above a ship's deck. The end of the hawser-like rope winding through these intricacies was then led to the windlass, and the huge lower block of the tackles was swung over the whale; to this block the great blubber hook, weighing some one hundred pounds, was attached. And now, suspended over the side on stages (planks slung from the ship as platforms), Starbuck and Stubb, the mates, armed with their long spades, began cutting a hole in the body for the insertion of the hook, just above the nearer of the two side-fins. This done, a broad, semicircular line is cut around the hole, the hook is inserted, and the main body of the crew, striking up a wild chorus, now begin heaving in one dense crowd at the windlass. Instantly the entire ship careens over on her side; every bolt in her starts like the nail-heads of an old house in frosty weather; she trembles, quivers, and nods her frightened mastheads to the sky. More and more she leans over to the whale, while every gasping heave of the windlass is answered by a helping heave from the waves; till at last a swift, startling snap is heard; with a great swash the ship rolls upward and backward from the whale, and the triumphant tackle rises into sight, dragging after it the loosened semicircular end of the first strip of blubber. Now, as the blubber envelops the whale precisely as the rind does an orange, so it is stripped off the body precisely as an orange is sometimes peeled — in a spiral. For the strain constantly kept up by the windlass keeps the whale rolling over and over in the water, and the blubber peels off in one even strip along the line called the "scarf," which is cut at the same time by the spades of Starbuck and Stubb, the mates; and just as fast as it is peeled off, and indeed by that very act, it is hoisted higher and higher aloft, until its upper end grazes the main-top. The men at the windlass then stop heaving, and for a moment or two the prodigious, blood-dripping mass sways to and fro as if let down from the sky, and everyone present must take good care to dodge it when it swings, or it may box his ears and pitch him headlong overboard.

One of the harpooners standing by now steps forward with a long, sharp weapon called a boarding-sword, waits for his moment, and deftly cuts a sizable hole in the lower part of the swinging mass. The end of the second of the two great alternating tackles is then hooked into this hole to keep a grip on the blubber and prepare for what comes next. Then this accomplished swordsman warns everyone to stand clear, makes one more scientific lunge at the mass, and with a few desperate, sidelong, slashing strokes cuts it clean in two. The short lower part stays fast, while the long upper strip, called a blanket-piece, swings free, ready to be lowered. The heavers forward now strike up their song again. While one tackle peels and hoists a second strip off the whale, the other is slowly eased off, and down goes the first strip through the main hatchway directly below, into a bare parlor called the blubber-room. In this twilight room a number of nimble hands keep coiling away the long blanket-piece as though it were a great living heap of braided snakes. And so the work goes on: the two tackles hoisting and lowering together; whale and windlass both heaving, the heavers singing, the blubber-room gentlemen coiling, the mates scarfing, the ship straining, and everyone swearing now and then to ease the general friction.
